---
title: "Permissions and auto mode"
---

Begin with ordinary prompts so you can see when the harness asks to read, edit, or execute. Read the proposed path and command before approving it. This makes approval fatigue visible.

After that observation, launch the next safe task from its lab directory with `opencode --auto` for the TUI. This auto-approves permissions that are not explicitly denied; an explicit `deny` remains. For a non-interactive prompt, use `opencode run --auto "<quoted prompt>"`. Check the [current OpenCode permissions documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/permissions/) before teaching a changed flag.

For a visual comparison, see the retained donor recordings for [OpenCode's GUI](../media/videos/opencode-gui.mp4) and [agent mode switching](../media/videos/agent-mode-switch-tab.mp4). The recordings are illustrative; current controls and names must be checked in the installed product.

::: {.callout-important}
Auto approval is convenience, not security. It does not stop a model from misunderstanding a task, following instructions in an untrusted file, sending prompt content to a provider, or finding an equivalent command path. Containers reduce host impact; they do not make sensitive data safe to disclose.
:::

Other agents use different names for approval bypass, auto mode, or sandbox removal. Do not transfer a flag between products. In Labs 2 and 3 you will compare an instruction, a permission prompt, a hook, and an actual environment boundary.

If a command or file access is surprising: deny it, record the path and reason, inspect `git diff`, and reset the disposable task folder using its README instructions. Never “test” a bypass against your laptop, credentials, or real research data.
